chapter_theme: The first half of Pattinathar's Thiruvekambamalai, twenty-five venbas each closing on the address கச்சியேகம்பனே. The poet turns on everything a householder holds, wife, children, kin, town, wealth, the body itself, and shows each as impermanent, as maya, or as the pit of the woman's body into which he fell; against them stand the Lord's feet, the five letters, the devotees, and the rare inward renouncer. Half the stanzas are confession or petition, half are rebukes of the ungiving and the lustful, and the Lord is asked why he made such people at all.
structure_note: No order is imposed; the stanzas alternate between self-reproach (242, 245, 247, 248, 250, 259), satire of others (252, 254, 255, 257, 260, 261) and short arguments (237, 240, 251, 253, 256). 245 and 264 (next chapter) share the whole closing line எல்லாப் பிழையும் பொறுத்தருள்வாய்; 249 and 277 run the same catalogue of town, kin, name, women, children, wealth. 255 and 261 use the same form, a list of what the wicked do not do, ending இருந்தென்ன, போயென்ன.

237.reading: Greater by crores than the man who does dharma is the man who has left his house; greater by a hundred crores than him is the man whose renunciation is in the heart; and of the one who forgot all, stayed in knowledge, and died free of both kinds of impression, the poet cannot tell the greatness.
237.nuance: The ladder has four rungs and the top one is inward and invisible: உள்ளத்துறவு, renunciation in the heart, outranks leaving the house, and the knower who has died free of இருவாதனை, the impressions of good and bad deeds, outranks even that. மறந்தான் அறக்காற்று is read as 'forgot completely'; the object forgotten is not named, and tradition supplies the world or the self.

238.reading: The wife and children who hug and embrace, when Time the carpenter cuts the body down like a tree, beat their breasts and wail; but once they have reached the edge of the cremation ground, will they step one step beyond it?
238.nuance: காலத்தச்சன், Time as carpenter, fells the body as a tree; the embrace of the first line and the single step of the last measure how far love goes. The question expects the answer no.

239.reading: The wife who, while the husband who holds her hand is asleep, lifts his hand, sets it down on the far side without stirring him, goes to the next compound, spends her sleep with another and comes back to sleep beside him: how, the poet asks, can he trust her?
239.nuance: The stanza is a scene, not an argument, and the poet's distrust of women elsewhere in the work (247, 250, 259, 260) rests on it. ஒப்புடன் (fittingly, or with a partner) and துயில் நீத்து (giving up sleep) leave the adultery implied rather than stated; tradition connects the stanza with the biography of Pattinathar's renunciation.

240.reading: A string puppet fitted with a good cord: if the cord fails, will it dance and tire itself? In the same way I move only by you, and if I were parted from you, is there anything I could do by myself?
240.nuance: The puppet confesses no agency apart from the Lord, which 290 in the Thiruthillai makes a doctrine: one in the hall makes all eat, sleep and dance on the rope of the two deeds. Here it is also a plea, since the poet is asking not to be parted.

241.reading: Apart from the company of the good, love of your worship and knowledge, is there any other standing? House, wealth, wife, kin, sons, livelihood and the fine body: all of it is an outer bewilderment.
241.nuance: வெளிமயக்கு, the bewilderment outside, sets what is within (company, love, knowledge) against what is outside; the same word returns at 265 for the painted women, and 253 ends on விழிமயக்கு, the eye's bewilderment.

242.reading: Wicked, not on the path, not a conqueror of the five senses, unlearned, one who does not go to the true devotees, does not speak the truth, has no love for your holy feet: why, the poet asks, was such a one as he born on earth?
242.nuance: Seven negatives in -ஆதவன் ending in a question about his own birth; the list is the poet's standard of a good life stated in the negative, with the devotees (மெய்யடியவர்) placed beside learning and truth.

243.reading: Nothing was brought at birth and nothing is carried away at death; what shall the poet say of the slaves who, not knowing that the wealth they mark as theirs in between was given by Siva and is to be given on, die holding it?
243.nuance: The argument makes wealth a loan between two empty-handed moments: since Siva gave it, giving it on is the only right use. குலாமர் (slaves) is the poet's word for those bound to possessions, as in Sivavakkiyar's use of the same word for those bound to outward authority.

244.reading: The thought of food is the one thought; when that is settled, the thought just named is a thought that never ends; the thought of fine-plumed women is the thought that returns many times: what thought, the poet asks the Lord, have you set in this sinful heart?
244.nuance: விசாரம் is repeated eight times and its sense shifts between care, worry and inquiry. The second line, சொன்ன விசாரம் தொலையா விசாரம், is the crux: 'the thought mentioned' may be the thought of food that goes on after eating, or may point forward to the thought of women; a few editors read the whole as a lament that the mind's cares are only food and women. The last line asks what the Lord intends by this, and may also mean 'what thought of yourself have you set in it?'

245.reading: The fault of not learning, of not reflecting, of not standing melted and weeping, of not meditating, of not saying your five letters, of not praising, of not worshipping: forgive every fault, the poet asks.
245.nuance: All seven faults are omissions in the inner and outer worship of the Lord; 264 in the next chapter repeats the closing line for faults of commission in speech, thought, deed and hearing.

246.reading: Leaving the deceitful friends and the women who are the undying mala, running outside, going with the mother who is true grace, then joining the father, and then forgetting the mother: that, he said, is nishtai.
246.nuance: An allegory of the path in family terms. Tradition takes the mother as grace or Shakti and the father as Siva, so that grace leads the soul to Siva and is then itself left behind; தாயை மறந்து, forgetting the mother, is the step that distinguishes the stanza. மாயா மலம் எனும் மாதர், women who are the mala that does not die, applies the Siddhanta term to women rather than to anava. என்றான், 'he said', attributes the teaching to another, perhaps the guru, and the stanza does not say who.

247.reading: Having gone into infatuation with women whose eyes are striped spears, the poet laments and does not say the five letters; and for whom is this lone body prey: the fox, the vulture and kite, the fierce dog, or the fire?
247.nuance: The body that lust cherished is auctioned among scavengers and the pyre; the question இரை எதற்கோ, prey for which, is left open as the only certainty. எழுத்தஞ்சும் சொலேன் makes the failure to recite the five letters the specific loss.

248.reading: The maya that comes before the poet's eyes showing itself as ear, nose and eye and calling itself a woman: this evil mind, which does not take it for the messenger Death sent but seeks it as its own home, how shall he describe?
248.nuance: The woman is dissolved into named parts and then into maya, and then into Yama's envoy: desire for her is the summons to death. ககமென்று in line 3 is corrupt and is read as அகமென்று, 'as home' or 'as self'; the sense of the stanza does not change with either.

249.reading: The town is not lasting, kin are not lasting, the name one has won is not lasting, nor women, nor children, nor glory, nor wealth, nor anyone in the country; your feet are what lasts.
249.nuance: சதம் (from Sanskrit sat, the real or permanent) is denied seven times and affirmed once. 277 runs the same list again with இருந்தென்ன, 'what if there is', so that the second stanza asks the use of what the first calls impermanent.

250.reading: Raging karma took the form of a woman, gathered and rounded into the breasts men speak of and into flesh, and by its cruelty pushed the poet into the great pit from which filth and blood tear and pour; he has not seen the bank by which to climb out.
250.nuance: The woman is not a person but வினை, deed, given a body; the பெருங்குழி is the vulva named by what flows from it, and ஏறும் கரை, the bank to climb, returns as the petition of 270. The stanza is as hostile to the female body as anything in the corpus and should be read as the poet's own state, not as doctrine.

251.reading: As men of means are known by their acts, warriors on the battlefield and the clear-minded by their faces, so those who have grace are to be recognised by their austerity, their nature, their grace and love, and even by their obscure words.
251.nuance: இருளுறு சொல், words wrapped in darkness, is the mark the stanza ends on: the speech of the graced is dark to others, a near description of the Siddhars' own cipher. The Kural's மறைமொழி (28) makes the same point for the great.

252.reading: Swelling their bellies like a cotton bale, they feed their own bellows with the six tastes, but will not take the trouble to feed those who have renounced; why, the poet asks, has the Lord kept such people on this wide earth?
252.nuance: துருத்தி, the bellows, is the belly as a leather bag, an image 263 applies to the whole body. The complaint is the renouncer's: he lives on what householders give, and the stanza is less about greed than about the failure of that obligation.

253.reading: As the sun that drives off the wicked dark is itself darkness to the owl's bird-eye, so what is plain in the hearts of the knowing is, for those who cannot know, only bewilderment; all is a bewilderment of the eye.
253.nuance: The owl is blind in light, so the light is not at fault; knowledge is present and the unknowing cannot see it. The last line, எல்லாம் விழிமயக்கே, can be the poet's summary (the whole world is an optical confusion) or the owl's view of the sun; both readings stand.

254.reading: They go to disputes and fights, come back and argue lawsuits, lend a hand to evil, daily find some gift to give to a woman and lose themselves in her, until their fate runs out: for what, the poet asks, were they born?
254.nuance: விதி மாளுமட்டும், until the allotted fate ends, sets a term on the life described, and the question ஏதுக்கு பிறந்தார் treats birth as something that should have a purpose.

255.reading: They lie without ceasing, revile the good, abuse the mother who bore them, commit a thousand treacheries, do not study the sastras, do no kindness to others and give nothing to those who come to them: what does it matter whether such people live or die?
255.nuance: இருந்தென்ன போயென்ன, what if they stay, what if they go, is the refrain of this stanza, 261 and (as இருந்தென்? இறந்தென்?) 277: the wicked and the useless are already as good as dead.

256.reading: Though water is white, it takes on without fail the nature of whatever ground it lies in and so comes to have many differing qualities; in the same way, says the stanza, I stand in souls unripe and ripe, my father the Lord.
256.nuance: The speaker of the last line is unclear. Read with எந்தைபிரான் as a vocative, the poet says he too stands in varying states as water does; read as the Lord's own word (இப்படியே நிற்பன்), the Lord stands in every soul coloured by its ripeness (பக்குவம்), the Siddhanta term for a soul's readiness for grace. The second reading is tradition's and fits the ripeness vocabulary better.

257.reading: A dog, when born, hunts well and gives pleasure; but why, the poet asks, did the Lord create men who, born from a mother's womb, are like a tree without fruit, a dried-up tank and a cow that gives no milk, men who do not give?
257.nuance: கம்பன்னராய்க் in line 2 is obscure; it may be a corrupt form or a jibe at Kamban as a byword for the self-important. The three similes are of things valued only for what they yield, and the dog, which at least hunts, is placed above the ungiving man.

258.reading: Do not let my love be like tamarind dissolved in a river; cherish it and hold it in your holy mind, you who burned the three cities, whose foot subdued Death, who hold the mountain as bow and the bull as banner.
258.nuance: ஆற்றில் கரைத்த புளி, tamarind dissolved in a river, is a stock figure for what is wasted without trace; the plea is that love offered to the Lord be kept, as the deeds named in the second half were kept.

259.reading: A deceitful demon came in the form of a woman, caught the poet, frightened him with her eyes, bewildered him with her breasts, pushed him into the sore-pit at her hips and stole the substance of his understanding; not thinking, he forgot the Lord.
259.nuance: போதப்பொருள் பறித்தல், stealing the substance of awareness, is the specific loss the stanza charges, and மறந்தேன், I forgot you, is its result. The woman as பிசாசு follows 248's maya and Death's messenger.

260.reading: They say sweet words to fill the tongue, 'if I am parted from you I shall die', and eat together; and when a man's hand runs dry they say 'go, come back' and hit him on the back of the head: is it the written fate of those who give to such women?
260.nuance: கை வறளின், when the hand dries, is the end of money; the blow to the back of the head is the dismissal. தலைவிதி, the fate written on the head, puns on the head that is struck.

261.reading: They do not learn Siva's story, do not speak the truth to the good even in a dream, do not give food to the hungry, do not stand by what the guru said, do not think of dharma, and have no thought at all of the Lord's name: tell me, what if they live, what if they die?
261.nuance: The list pairs with 255; here the omissions are of devotion and dharma, with the guru's word and the Lord's name as the last two. கனவிலும், even in a dream, is the Kural's measure of a settled nature (819, 1054).

links.note: Both measure the kin's love by where they stop: Tirumular's wailing wives and children turn back at the edge of the town while others strip and burn him; Pattinathar's embracing wife and children wail but will not take one step past the edge of the cremation ground.
Sivavakkiyar asks whether children, wives and kin, all maya, can come along when Death calls; Pattinathar answers with the scene: they reach the cremation ground and go no further.

Both use the puppet made to dance: Tirumular says Hara's grace makes the spread elements dance like a false puppet and thereby settles the soul; Pattinathar says he is the string puppet and can do nothing if the cord that is the Lord fails. Tirumular describes the five acts, Pattinathar pleads not to be parted.

The Naladiyar says nothing goes with a person but their deeds, not even the body they adorned; Pattinathar says nothing was brought at birth and nothing is taken at death, and draws from it that the wealth held in between is Siva's and is to be given.

On the allegorical reading both share, mother as grace or Shakti and father as Siva, they part on the end: Tirumular says that once the conceit of 'my mother, my father' is gone, the Lord joined with her stands as the mother after, so the Mother remains; Pattinathar's nishtai goes with the mother to the father and then forgets the mother. The conflict depends on taking Pattinathar's தாயை மறந்து as a final state and not a stage.

Both leave the cherished body to scavengers: Arunagirinathar tends a body that ghosts, vultures, jackals and crows will tear and drag; Pattinathar asks whether his is prey for the fox, the vulture and kite, the dog or the fire. In both the body was cherished through lust.

Tirumular says kin is one and God is one, and there is no refuge outside one's own mind; Pattinathar denies permanence to town, kin, name, women, children, glory, wealth and everyone in the country and gives it to the Lord's feet alone. Both reduce the whole circle of belonging to one holding.

The Naladiyar lists entrails, fat, blood, bone, sinew, skin and flesh and asks which part is the garlanded woman; Pattinathar says karma itself took the form of a woman, became the breasts and flesh men speak of, and threw him into the pit of filth and blood. Both dissolve the woman into her body; Pattinathar adds that he fell in.

The Kural says the greatness of those whose word is full is shown by their hidden words (மறைமொழி); Pattinathar says the graced may be known by their austerity, nature, grace and love and even by their obscure words (இருளுறு சொல்). Both make the dark saying a sign of the great rather than a defect.

Arunagirinathar's miser sends the poor ascetic who asks for food from the upper house to the lower and leaps at him like a dog; Pattinathar's householders stuff their own bellies with the six tastes and will not trouble to feed the renounced. Both are written from the side of the mendicant.

Both say water takes the nature of the ground it lies in; the Kural applies it to understanding, which takes the nature of one's company, and Pattinathar to the Lord or the soul, which stands in each soul according to its ripeness. The image is the same, the domain different.

The Kural says the wealth of one who gives nothing to the destitute is like a beautiful woman growing old alone; Pattinathar likens the ungiving man to a fruitless tree, a dried tank and a cow without milk and asks why he was created. Both judge a life by what it yields to others.

Tirumular says even those who have grasped the meaning and hold the flash of light are infatuated with women who bewilder, and a mind once bewildered cannot be changed; Pattinathar says the demon in woman's form bewildered him with her breasts and stole the substance of his understanding, so that he forgot the Lord.

Sivavakkiyar says people have lost themselves in the bewilderment cast by women with collyrium-dark eyes and can be saved only by a mind that has known truth; Pattinathar says the woman's eyes frightened and her breasts bewildered him and robbed him of awareness. Both name the eyes and the loss of knowing.

The same sequence in both: Arunagirinathar's courtesans melt a man while his wealth lasts and, when it ends, beat him and drive him out; Pattinathar's women swear they would die if parted and, when his hand runs dry, say 'go and come' and strike the back of his head.

source_issues: 248 line 3 ககமென்று is corrupt; the sense requires அகமென்று.
257 line 2 கம்பன்னராய்க் cannot be construed with confidence.
The ids are the work's own numbering (thiruvekambamalai:1 to 25); the unit printed as 279 in the next chapter is unnumbered (u1) and is a different metre.
